title: Efficient Attention: Heads, Memory Traffic, and Context
summary: Distinguish attention architecture from kernel optimization, calculate KV-cache capacity, and defend long-context design choices using shapes, bandwidth, and quality evidence.
learningObjectives: Derive MHA, MQA, and GQA tensor shapes and cache requirements.
Explain why exact IO-aware attention remains quadratic in arithmetic.
Separate positional context extension from reliable long-range reasoning.
Choose dense or sparse attention using workload-specific evidence.

sections.title: Three budgets hidden behind efficient attention
paragraphs: Attention is the step inside each transformer layer where every token looks back at other tokens to decide which ones matter (the Inside a decoder: from text to the next token article walks through it). It is also where long prompts start to get expensive, so a lot of engineering goes into making it cheaper. The catch is that "efficient attention" is an umbrella term rather than one optimization. It can mean reducing persistent state (the keys and values a model keeps around between generation steps, usually called the KV cache), avoiding temporary memory traffic (moving large intermediate score tables in and out of GPU memory), or removing query-key interactions (letting each token look at fewer other tokens). These target different budgets and carry different correctness implications. A good opening move in an interview answer is to ask whether the workload is training, prompt ingestion (often called prefill, where the model reads the whole prompt in one pass), or token generation (decode, where it produces one token at a time). A design that accelerates a long prompt may barely affect the next-token latency of a short conversation, especially when reading model weights dominates the step.

To see where each budget comes from, it helps to write down the shapes. As a quick reminder, each position produces a query (what it is looking for) plus a key and a value (what it offers to others), and attention scores come from comparing queries against keys. For batch size B (the number of sequences processed together), query length Tq, key length Tk, query-head count Hq, and head width d, dense attention forms scores with shape [B, Hq, Tq, Tk]. During full-sequence training or prefill, both lengths grow with the sequence, so score arithmetic grows quadratically. During cached autoregressive decoding (generating one token at a time while reusing the stored keys and values of earlier tokens), Tq is usually one and Tk is the retained history. Each new step therefore grows linearly with history length, although generating an entire long continuation accumulates more work across steps.

With those shapes in hand, try to keep three quantities separate on a whiteboard: projection and attention FLOPs, temporary score/probability storage, and persistent key-value state. Optimizing one does not automatically optimize the others. The attention output must still flow through an output projection and the rest of the transformer block. Measure end-to-end latency because even a large attention-kernel improvement can produce a modest application improvement when another component consumes most of the time. The figure at the end of this section sketches which budget tends to be the tight one in prefill, decode and training.
sections.formula: O = softmax(QKᵀ / √d + mask)V; score shape = [B, Hq, Tq, Tk]

sections.title: MHA, MQA, and GQA change the key-value head count
paragraphs: Let's start with the persistent state budget. Attention is normally split into several heads, smaller attention computations that run side by side, each with its own view of the tokens. Multi-head attention (MHA) gives each query head its own key and value head. Multi-query attention (MQA) shares one key-value head across all query heads. Grouped-query attention (GQA) sits between them: multiple query heads share each key-value head. The GQA paper investigates this quality-efficiency compromise and conversion through additional training. Head sharing changes the model parameterization; it is not generally an interchangeable inference flag for an arbitrary trained MHA checkpoint. A rough analogy: think of query heads as students and KV heads as textbooks. MHA gives every student their own copy, MQA has the whole class share one, and GQA puts students in small groups that each share a copy. Everyone still writes their own answer. The walkthrough below shows four query heads regrouping onto fewer stored K/V pairs while the four output heads stay separate.

To make this concrete, suppose the model width is 4096, Hq is 32, and d is 128. Queries have shape [B, Tq, 32, 128]. With eight KV heads, each of K and V has shape [B, Tk, 8, 128], and four query heads use each KV head. Ignoring bias, the query projection matrix Wq has shape [4096, 4096], while the key and value projections Wk and Wv each have shape [4096, 1024]. The output before its projection still concatenates 32 query-head results into width 4096. Sharing K and V does not merge the query outputs. The figure at the end of this section lays out the MHA, GQA and MQA patterns for these 32 query heads.

One implementation detail is worth watching. The grouped kernel (the GPU routine that actually computes attention) should reuse each KV head without physically duplicating the cache into 32 heads. An explicit repeat may be useful as a correctness reference, but materializing it can erase memory savings. Check both stored tensor layouts and temporary allocations. Head partitioning across devices adds another constraint: a chosen tensor-parallel layout (splitting a layer's heads across several GPUs, covered in the Mixture of Experts and Parallelism article) may replicate KV heads when there are fewer KV heads than participating ranks. Global logical cache size and per-device allocated memory are then different numbers.
sections.formula: group size = Hq / Hkv; Q: [B,Tq,Hq,d]; K,V: [B,Tk,Hkv,d] (assume Hq divisible by Hkv)

sections.title: Calculate cache bytes before promising concurrency
paragraphs: Now that the KV head count is clear, we can turn it into bytes, which is what really decides how many requests fit on a GPU. For uniform layers and equal-length requests, count two tensors per layer (K and V), multiply by layers, active sequences, retained tokens, KV heads, head width, and bytes per element. Use retained tokens rather than the advertised maximum context unless preallocation actually reserves the maximum. For heterogeneous lengths, replace B times T with the sum of retained lengths. This arithmetic describes logical KV payload, not the full device allocation. The formula box below writes the whole product out.

Here is a worked example. Consider 32 layers, eight simultaneous sequences, 8192 retained tokens each, eight KV heads, width 128, and two-byte elements. The product is 8,589,934,592 bytes, exactly 8 GiB using 2³⁰ bytes per GiB. Each retained token in one sequence costs 131,072 bytes across all layers, or 128 KiB. At identical settings, 32-head MHA consumes 32 GiB and one-head MQA consumes 1 GiB. These are calculated capacities, not benchmark observations, and the bar chart at the end of this section puts the three side by side.

If only 12 GiB remains after reserving weights, workspace, and other allocations, the ideal GQA payload permits twelve such sequences. In practice, admitting requests takes more headroom than that. Many serving systems hand out cache memory in fixed-size blocks (the Serving LLMs: KV Cache as a Memory and Latency Budget article covers this), so production admission must reserve room for cache blocks, partially filled blocks, metadata, and growth as outputs are generated. A request admitted at 8192 tokens may grow past that length. Cache quantization (storing K and V in fewer bits, discussed in the Quantization and Compression article) changes bytes per element but introduces scale metadata and possible quality loss. Prefix sharing (reusing cache entries for a common prompt prefix, such as a shared system prompt) can reduce physical allocation, but only count it when the allocator actually shares identical prefixes.

sections.title: FlashAttention changes IO, not dense connectivity
paragraphs: So far we have looked at persistent state. The second budget is temporary memory traffic, and this is where FlashAttention comes in. A GPU has a large main memory (called HBM) that is relatively slow to reach and a small amount of very fast on-chip memory. A straightforward implementation writes the score matrix and probabilities to high-bandwidth memory (HBM). FlashAttention tiles the computation (splits it into small blocks) that fit in fast on-chip memory, carrying running softmax statistics and output accumulators. It avoids storing the complete quadratic intermediate. An analogy that might help: instead of hauling a giant spreadsheet between a warehouse and your desk, you bring over a few pages at a time, do all the work on them, and keep only a running tally. Training can reconstruct needed blocks during the backward pass (the gradient computation) rather than saving every probability. Extra arithmetic can therefore reduce elapsed time by eliminating expensive memory transfers.

The tricky part is softmax, which normalizes each score row by a sum over every key in that row, so it seems to need the whole row at once. The fix is an online softmax. For a row, track its running maximum m, exponential sum l, and unnormalized weighted-value sum u. When a new block changes the maximum, rescale the old sums before combining them with the block. Dividing u by l after processing all permitted keys gives the same mathematical softmax result. Averaging independent block softmax outputs would be wrong because each block has a different denominator. The walkthrough below streams a toy four-key row through two tiles and shows exactly this rescaling, including what naive averaging would get wrong.

Exact means the same dense attention operation, subject to floating-point rounding differences from changed reduction order. FlashAttention does not make dense attention linear-time: query-key arithmetic remains quadratic for full sequences. Its storage benefit also does not remove the persistent decoding KV cache. Sparse or low-rank attention instead changes which interactions are represented or how they are approximated; those changes need separate quality evaluation (sparse windows get their own section below). The figure at the end of this section summarizes the streaming steps.
sections.formula: m′ = max(m, mb); l′ = exp(m−m′)l + exp(mb−m′)lb; u′ = exp(m−m′)u + exp(mb−m′)ub; O = u/l

sections.title: RoPE supports relative structure, not unlimited reliable context
paragraphs: Next, let's switch from memory to context length. Attention on its own has no sense of word order, so position has to be injected somehow. Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) rotate pairs of query and key coordinates by position-dependent angles. Their dot product (the attention score) depends on relative rotation, making relative position available inside attention scores. Picture two clock hands: if you advance both by the same amount, the angle between them does not change, and that angle is what the score sees. The walkthrough below shows one coordinate pair doing exactly this. Different coordinate pairs use different frequencies, or rotation speeds. RoPE changes positional representation rather than the number of tokens stored or the number of attention interactions. Its mathematical definition can be evaluated beyond training positions without guaranteeing useful model behavior there.

That raises a natural question: how do you stretch a model past the context length it was trained on? One approach, position interpolation, compresses a longer range of positions into the range used during training; the paper listed in the sources combines this with fine-tuning. Changing frequency schedules or position scaling similarly changes the geometry the model sees. These choices can trade long-distance behavior against fine positional distinctions. The appropriate question is whether a specific model and extension recipe preserve accuracy across the target distances and tasks, not whether a configuration file accepts a larger integer.

So how would you check whether an extension actually works? One approach is to design an evaluation matrix with short prompts, progressively longer prompts, and evidence placed near the beginning, middle, and end. Include multi-hop dependencies and contradictory distractors rather than only exact retrieval. Keep the tokenizer, position convention, cache representation, and scaling settings consistent between prefill and decode. Reusing a prefix cache produced under different positional settings can invalidate the intended attention computation. A successful memory allocation demonstrates capacity, while stable task accuracy demonstrates usable context. The figure at the end of this section lays out these validation steps.
sections.formula: q̃p = R(p)q; k̃t = R(t)k; q̃pᵀk̃t = qᵀR(t−p)k (for compatible rotation blocks)

sections.title: Sliding windows exchange direct reach for bounded work
paragraphs: The last lever goes after the third budget from the start of this article: the query-key interactions themselves. Sliding-window attention restricts each query to a neighborhood of nearby tokens, a bit like reading a long book while only being able to glance back at the last page or two. Longformer, an earlier long-document model, combines local windows with selected global attention positions; its encoder pattern (where tokens can look both forward and backward) should not be mistaken for a causal decoder mask. In a causal decoder with window W including the current token, position t can directly access positions max(0, t−W+1) through t. Each query has at most W keys, making attention work proportional to T times W for fixed head dimensions. The walkthrough below starts from a full causal mask, narrows it to a window of two, and then adds one global key.

A nice side effect shows up in memory. If every layer uses that causal window, a rolling cache (one that drops the oldest entry as each new token arrives) can discard positions outside it, bounding retained state per layer. Layers using global attention still require their own longer state. Across stacked local layers, information can travel farther than one window, but this indirect path is not equivalent to direct retrieval of arbitrary old tokens. Hidden states are finite representations; an early account identifier may not survive the intermediate transformations needed to answer a late exact-match question.

Beyond simple windows, other sparse patterns add selected global tokens, dilated links (connections that skip positions at regular intervals), or blocks. They alter the communication graph and must preserve causality when used for generation. Fewer mathematical edges do not guarantee faster kernels: irregular indexing, poor tile utilization, and data movement can erase the savings. Start with a pattern the model was trained to use, then measure both application quality and actual execution. Removing old cache entries from a dense model is a behavioral change, even if it prevents an out-of-memory error. The figure at the end of this section compares the dense, local, and local-plus-global graphs.
sections.formula: Allowed causal keys(t) = {j : max(0,t−W+1) ≤ j ≤ t}; total edges ≤ T × W

sections.title: Defend the combination with a falsifiable experiment
paragraphs: In practice you will rarely pick just one of these. The good news is that these techniques compose because they address different dimensions. A checkpoint trained with GQA can use an IO-aware exact kernel (FlashAttention-style) while keeping dense causal connectivity and a validated positional configuration. A model trained for local attention can combine head sharing with a window-aware kernel. Avoid describing the whole combination as lossless: exact kernel substitution has a different semantic status from changing the checkpoint's head sharing, positional behavior, or connectivity.

To back a design up, benchmark realistic prompt and output length distributions at fixed quality targets. Report time to first token, inter-token latency, throughput, peak allocated memory, and failure rate across concurrency levels. Separate warm execution from compilation and initialization. Compare numerics against a small reference attention implementation with representative masks and unequal query/key lengths. Do not infer an end-to-end speedup directly from a fourfold cache reduction: lower bytes can enable more batching, but the resulting latency depends on scheduling, other kernels, and hardware. A defensible design states what would cause you to reject it.

interview.question: A 32-layer decoder has 32 query heads of width 128. Eight requests each retain 8192 tokens. With two-byte KV elements, MHA exhausts a 12 GiB cache budget. Propose a design without promising untested quality or speed.
interview.answer: The MHA logical payload is 32 GiB. A checkpoint trained with eight KV heads reduces it to 8 GiB, leaving 4 GiB for cache overhead and growth within the stated cache budget. I would use a compatible exact IO-aware kernel, validate mask and position correctness, and benchmark prefill and decode separately. I would not convert the checkpoint by merely changing its head-count configuration. If future context growth exceeds budget, I would evaluate admission limits, KV quantization, or a model trained for local attention, each against task quality. RoPE scaling alone does not reduce cache bytes or prove reliable long-context answers.

pitfalls: Counting query heads rather than KV heads in the cache formula.
Calling FlashAttention approximate or claiming its dense arithmetic is linear.
Treating a logical payload estimate as an allocator admission guarantee.
Expanding GQA K/V tensors physically and accidentally losing the savings.
Equating a larger RoPE configuration with validated long-context quality.
Applying an encoder's symmetric local mask to a causal decoder.
Assuming a rolling cache is valid for layers trained with global attention.
checklist: Write Q, K, V, and score shapes with distinct query and KV head counts.
Calculate bytes using actual retained lengths, dtype, layers, and physical sharding.
Reserve capacity for generation growth and allocator overhead.
Verify causal masking and position IDs for both prefill and cached decode.
Confirm the checkpoint supports its sharing pattern and positional configuration.
Measure quality by evidence distance and test short-context regressions.
Benchmark latency, throughput, and memory at realistic concurrency.
State which changes preserve the attention operation and which require quality validation.

flashcards.front: What three budgets should an efficient-attention discussion separate?
flashcards.back: Arithmetic, temporary score/probability storage, and persistent KV state. Optimizations affect different budgets, so one memory improvement does not imply a proportional latency improvement.

flashcards.front: What are GQA Q, K, and V shapes?
flashcards.back: Q is [B,Tq,Hq,d]; K and V are [B,Tk,Hkv,d]. Hkv can be smaller than Hq because groups of query heads share keys and values.

flashcards.front: How do MHA, GQA, and MQA differ?
flashcards.back: MHA has one KV head per query head; MQA has one shared KV head; GQA uses an intermediate number. Query heads still produce separate outputs.

flashcards.front: With 32 query heads and eight KV heads, how many query heads share one KV head?
flashcards.back: Four. The ratio Hq/Hkv determines group size, while attention still computes a separate result for every query head.

flashcards.front: Derive the logical KV-cache size for equal-length sequences.
flashcards.back: 2 × layers × batch × retained tokens × KV heads × head width × bytes per element. The factor two counts both K and V; query heads do not determine stored KV size.

flashcards.front: Why does the worked GQA example use 8 GiB?
flashcards.back: 2 × 32 × 8 × 8192 × 8 × 128 × 2 equals 8,589,934,592 bytes, or 8 GiB. It excludes weights, workspace, and allocation overhead.

flashcards.front: Why is logical cache payload insufficient for admission control?
flashcards.back: Physical allocation includes partially filled blocks, metadata, possible replication, and future output growth. Reserving only the current payload can cause later allocation failure.

flashcards.front: In what sense is FlashAttention exact?
flashcards.back: It computes the same masked softmax attention operation through tiling and shared normalization. Reduction order can change floating-point rounding, so exact does not mean bitwise identical.

flashcards.front: Why cannot independent block softmax outputs simply be averaged?
flashcards.back: Their denominators differ. Running maxima, exponential sums, and weighted values must be rescaled and combined to represent one normalization across all allowed keys.

flashcards.front: Does FlashAttention remove quadratic dense attention work?
flashcards.back: No. It avoids storing the full score matrix and reduces memory traffic, but full-sequence dense attention still evaluates quadratically many query-key interactions.

flashcards.front: Why does RoPE not guarantee unlimited usable context?
flashcards.back: The rotation formula can accept new positions, but the model may not generalize to their positional relationships. Extension needs task evaluation and often an adapted positional recipe or training.

flashcards.front: When can a sliding-window decoder use bounded KV state?
flashcards.back: A layer can discard keys it can never attend to again under its trained window pattern. Global layers still need longer state, and imposing eviction on a dense model changes behavior.

flashcards.front: Why is a multilayer local receptive field not equivalent to global attention?
flashcards.back: Distant information must survive intermediate hidden representations. An indirect path can carry useful summaries without preserving every detail required for exact distant retrieval.

flashcards.front: Why might a fourfold KV reduction yield little latency gain?
flashcards.back: Weight reads, other kernels, communication, or scheduling may dominate. Cache reduction changes capacity and potential bandwidth demand; end-to-end speed must be measured for the actual workload.
